header: (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer
Present: Malik Waseem Fazal, Advocate for
body: SYED MUDASSER AMEER, J.- Through this revision petition, the petitioners call in question the judgment and decree dated 12.11.2008 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-V, Mansehra, whereby, on acceptance of respondents’ appeal, Suit No.145/1 of 2003 was decreed, while setting aside the judgment and __________________________________________ (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer decree dated 23.12.2005 passed by the learned trial Court dismissing the suit.

2. The lis involves a long chain of events. Initially, the suit property was owned by Hindus. After partition of the subcontinent, it became evacuee property and was transferred in favour of the Central Government vide mutation No.2052 dated 20.04.1960. Thereafter, it was allotted in favour of Sultan Muhammad son of Abdul Ghani through R.L-II No.6 and mutation No.3262 dated 20.06.1969. Subsequently, the property was transferred in favour of Umar Khan son of Wali Muhammad Khan vide sale mutation No.4024 dated 28.08.1975.

3. This sale/transfer was pre-empted by Jehandad, father of the respondents, through Suit No.76/1 of 1976, wherein a compromise decree dated 20.07.1976 was passed in his favour, followed by mutation No.4084 dated 20.04.1977. Jehandad later transferred the suit property through gift mutation No.4389 dated 17.02.1982 in favour of Chanzeb, the present respondent.

4. There was, however, another significant development. The allotment of the suit property in __________________________________________ (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer favour of Sultan Muhammad was cancelled by the Chief Settlement Commissioner (Lands), Hazara vide order dated 24.06.1974 after an inquiry. This order was challenged by Sultan through W.P. No.32/72 on the ground, inter alia, that it had been passed without affording an opportunity of hearing. The writ petition was accepted by this Court on 30.03.1983 and the matter was remanded for fresh decision.
5. Subsequently, however, the legal heirs of Sultan, through their attorney, admitted the correctness of the cancellation order dated 24.06.1974 and withdrew their claim.
Consequently, vide order dated 05.06.1985 passed by the Assistant Commissioner/Collector, Mansehra, the withdrawal was allowed and the cancellation order stood restored.

6. In the wake thereof, the suit property reverted to the Central Government vide mutation No.4679 dated 26.09.1989. It was thereafter allotted/transferred in favour of Muhammad Mohsin of Rawalpindi vide mutation No.4604 dated 26.09.1989. Subsequently, it was transferred through sale in favour of Munawar __________________________________________ (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer Hussain son of Jumma Khan and petitioner No.1 vide mutation No.4835 dated 28.03.1990. Later, it was transferred in favour of Jumma Khan vide mutation No.5036 dated 20.10.1993 and thereafter in favour of petitioner No.2 vide mutation No.5037 dated 20.10.1993.

7. Upon noticing these adverse entries, the respondents instituted the suit, which was contested by the present petitioners. After fullfledged trial, the learned trial Court dismissed the suit vide judgment and decree dated 23.12.2005. The appeal preferred by the respondents was, however, accepted, and the suit was decreed, giving rise to the present revision petition.
8. Heard. Record perused.

9. The respondents claim ownership on the basis of gift mutation No.4389 dated 17.02.1982, derived from Jehandad, who himself based his title upon the pre-emption decree dated 20.07.1976 arising out of mutation No.4024 dated 28.08.1975.

10. The pivotal question, however, is whether Sultan Muhammad, the original allottee, possessed a valid title capable of transmission. __________________________________________ (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer 11. The record leaves no manner of doubt that Sultan Muhammad’s allotment stood cancelled vide order dated 24.06.1974 passed by the Chief Settlement Commissioner (Lands), Hazara. Though the matter was once remanded by this Court, the legal heirs of Sultan subsequently admitted the correctness of the cancellation order, which was restored on 05.06.1985.

12. In such circumstances, the very foundation of the respondents’ title stands extinguished. Once the allotment in favour of Sultan Muhammad ceased to exist, any subsequent transfer, including the sale in favour of Umar Khan, the pre-emption decree in favour of Jehandad, and the gift in favour of the respondents, cannot survive.

13. It is settled law that a transferee can acquire no better title than that of his predecessor. If the title of the vendor collapses, the transferee must also fall with it. Reliance in this regard is placed on Talib Hussain v. Member, Board of Revenue (2003 SCMR 549) and Rasheed Ahmad v. Additional Commissioner (Rev.) (2007 CLC 1801).

(S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer 14. There is yet another legal impediment. Section 25 of the Displaced Persons (Land Settlement) Act, 1958 expressly ousts the jurisdiction of Civil Courts in matters relating to orders passed under sections 10 and 11 of the said Act. Since the cancellation of allotment was effected under these provisions, the respondents could not have challenged the same before a Civil Court. Reliance is placed on Syed Abdul Hakim v. Muhammad Azam Khan (1991 CMR 1976).

15. Similarly, the suit property being evacuee property, the jurisdiction of Civil Courts is further barred under section 14 of the Evacuee Trust Properties (Management and Disposal) Act, 1975. In this respect, reliance is placed on Evacuee Trust Property Board v. Ahmed (2004 SCMR 440).

16. The contention of the respondents that their title flows from a pre-emption decree does not advance their case. A pre-emption decree merely substitutes the pre-emptor in place of the vendee. It does not validate or cure defects in the title of the original transferor. Reliance is placed __________________________________________ (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer on Muhammad Hayat v. Settlement Commissioner (Land), Lahore (2001 CLC 1537).

17. Likewise, the argument that the decree in favour of the respondents remains intact is misconceived. The pre-emption decree did nothing more than place Jehandad in the shoes of Umar Khan. It had no bearing on the validity of the original allotment, which had already been cancelled.

18. It is also a settled principle that where the foundational order is without lawful authority, the entire superstructure built thereon cannot be sustained. Reference may be made to Executive District Officer (Education), Rawalpindi v. Muhammad Younas (2007 SCMR 1835) and Amna Bibi v. Sona Khan (2012 YLR 2047).

19. The learned appellate Court decreed the suit primarily on the reasoning that petitioner No.2 is the real brother of Sultan Muhammad. This reasoning is wholly insufficient. The respondents have failed to establish any nexus between Sultan Muhammad and Muhammad Mohsin, in whose favour the property was subsequently allotted in 1989. The petitioners, on __________________________________________ (S.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Syed Mudasser Ameer the other hand, derive their title from said Mohsin, whose allotment remained valid at the relevant time.
20. Thus, the reasoning adopted by the learned appellate Court is not sustainable in law or on facts.

21. For what has been discussed above, this revision petition is allowed. The judgment and decree dated 12.11.2008 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-V, Mansehra are set aside, and the judgment and decree dated 23.12.2005 passed by the learned trial Court dismissing the suit are restored.
ANNOUNCED.
J U D G E
